title: Remember me as awake
hookLine: Dona asks: are you a god? a spirit? a human? No: awake

cards: A road between two towns. A brahmin named Dona is walking along it, and he stops. In the dust are footprints, and inside each print, the text says, is the mark of a wheel with a thousand spokes, rim and hub complete.
These can't be the footprints of a human being, he thinks. So he follows them, off the road, to the foot of a tree, where someone is sitting, calm, senses at rest, mind at peace.
Dona walks up and asks a very direct question.

teach.h: A GOD? A SPIRIT? A HUMAN? NO.
teach.b: It comes in four parts. Will you be a god? No, brahmin.
A gandhabba, a heavenly musician? No. A yakkha, a spirit of the forest?
No. A human being, then? No, brahmin, I will not be a human being.
Dona is baffled: then what will you be?
The things that would make him a god, a spirit or a human, the Buddha explains, are the taints, the deep habits of craving and confusion that push a being into one kind of life or another.
In him those are abandoned, cut at the root like a palm stump, unable to grow again. Then a picture.
A blue or red or white lotus is born in the water, grows up in the water, and rises above it, and the water doesn't cling to it.
In the same way, he says, he was born and grew up in the world, but has gone beyond it, and the world doesn't stain him.
Then the line: remember me, brahmin, as a buddha. Buddha isn't a name. It's a title: awake, the one who has woken up.
Notice what the answer refuses. It won't be filed under any category Dona brought with him. It doesn't claim divinity, and it doesn't settle for being just another person.
It points to a state: not asleep. Teachers often use this sutta when someone asks whether Buddhists worship the Buddha as a god. The Buddha's own answer, here, is no.

how: Buddhist teachers often tell the Dona story to explain the title buddha, 'the awakened one,' and many Buddhists bow to Buddha images as a sign of respect for that awakening rather than as worship of a god.

o: the family name of a prince
one who has woken up, awake
a god who came down to earth

games.q: remember me as awake: tap the pairs.
p: the brahmin who followed the footprints
each marked with a thousand-spoked wheel
the one who has woken up

s: in this sutta the Buddha says he is a god
he says no to god, to gandhabba, to yakkha, and even to 'human being.'
the Buddha compares himself to a lotus standing above the water
born and grown in the world, but not stained by it.
buddha is a family name, like Gotama
Gotama is the clan name; buddha is a title meaning awake.

games.q: you're Dona. a stranger sits under a tree, and his footprints carry marks no ordinary person has. what do you do?
o: walk on; it's none of your business.
ask him plainly what kind of being he is.
bow and ask him for a blessing.
games.why: Dona asks straight out: god, spirit or human? the answer to all three is no, and the real answer is a word: awake.

practice: Let your eyes rest and, for a few breaths, notice whether part of you is half asleep: running a plan, replaying a talk, waiting for the next thing.

Then wake up fully to this one moment, the weight of your body, the air on your skin, the sound nearest you. When you drift, that's fine; the drifting is how you learn what waking feels like, so come back and wake again.

wordCard.voice: buddha. The Pali word for 'one who has awakened,' the Buddha's answer to the brahmin Dona: not a god, not a spirit, not merely human, but buddha. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali buddha: past participle of budh, to wake up or to know; 'one who has awakened.'

carryVoice: Your line: be awake for one moment. Like the lotus, risen clear of the water it grew in. Until tomorrow.
